chapter.title: Nobody Could Hear the Reading
chapter.sub: The user experiences one room, not your org chart.

items.text: SEASON 1 · EPISODE 6 · DRAFT  Commissioning trial · Maya and Avery · Level L2 (Operator)  The room sounds fine. But the people using the assistive listening receivers hear nothing during the scripture reading.

items.title: The Silent Reading
items.stakes: People on the listening system hear the songs — never the scripture. For nine years, nobody said anything because everybody assumed it was them.
items.reward: Every output with an owner. Mr. Adeyemi hears the reading for the first time in eleven years.

objectives.text: Find out when the silence starts
Give the listening system its own mix
Name the two good decisions that collided
Prove it the way Dolores lives it
Look closer: find two people nobody asked

items.rumor: Nine years ago Ray patched something. He remembers why. Nobody else does.

items.alt: Dolores in the booth, holding the assistive listening receiver.

bubbles.text: The songs came through fine. Then Ana read the scripture, and — nothing. I thought it was me again.
It isn't you. Let's find out what it is.

items.alt: Mr. Tunde Adeyemi, another receiver user, waits his turn with the same complaint.

bubbles.text: Same here. Every week I hear the band. Never the readings. I assumed that was how it worked.

items.caption: Nobody had complained, because everybody assumed it was them.

lines.text: I assumed that was how it worked. Songs yes, words no. Like a radio station with opinions.

items.title: Eleven years of initials
items.body: Mr. Adeyemi signs out receiver 4 every week. In eleven years, no one has ever asked him how it sounds. In the comments column, once, in 2016: *ok.*

items.alt: Maya checks a receiver at the booth while the band rehearses. Music comes through clearly.
items.caption: At the booth, during a song: the receiver works perfectly.

items.prompt: Two people hear the songs but never the readings. What do you do first?
items.happening: Receiver users hear music but not speech.
unknown: Where the listening system gets its sound
items.risk: Everyone who depends on a receiver — people who've stopped asking.

hints.text: Test at the moment it fails, not the moment it works.
What's different about the room during a reading?
Run the whole service order with a receiver on.
If it goes silent at one button, ask what that button changes.
Walkthrough, then a variant: an overflow room that loses audio only during announcements.

options.label: Replace the receiver batteries
options.result: New batteries. The receiver still works — during the song Maya tests it with.
options.consequence: “Must be fixed.” Next Sunday's reading is silent again.

options.label: Listen through every scene
options.result: Maya wears a receiver and runs the service order: worship, reading, sermon, worship.
options.consequence: Silence starts exactly when SPOKEN WORD is pressed.

options.label: Turn the transmitter up
options.result: The songs get louder in the receivers.
options.consequence: The readings are still silent — just louder silence.

options.label: Suggest they sit closer
options.consequence: The problem is handed back to the people it's hurting.
options.fail: The problem gets handed back to the people it's hurting.

items.alt: Tuesday. Maya wears a receiver and has Lily run the service order from the booth: worship, reading, sermon, worship. The receiver goes silent exactly when SPOKEN WORD is pressed.
items.caption: Silence begins exactly when SPOKEN WORD is pressed.

items.alt: Lily, at the touch panel, connects it to last month.

bubbles.text: We pressed every preset after the rack fix. They all worked.
We checked the mics going in. We never checked every place the sound comes out.

items.text: Act I — “Every output, against its intent”

items.caption: Every output, and the person it's for.

items.title: The listening system was always on the wrong mix
items.body: Nine years ago the listening transmitter was patched to AUX 4 — the band's monitor mix — because it was the only mix with speech. Then someone built SPOKEN WORD to mute the wedges. Two good decisions, years apart, silenced every reading.

items.alt: In the rack, the listening transmitter's input cable carries a masking-tape label: 'from AUX 4'.
items.caption: The listening system is fed from AUX 4.

items.alt: System View: a routing map. The lectern, pastor, vocal and band feed the MAIN bus to the room speakers. AUX 4, the band monitor mix, feeds the band wedges — and, through a dashed line, the listening transmitter. In SPOKEN WORD, AUX 4 is muted, so the transmitter goes silent.
items.caption: AUX 4 is the band's monitor mix. SPOKEN WORD mutes it so the wedges don't ring during the sermon — and the listening system goes silent with it.

items.text: 🔭 PHYSICS IN MOTION  Reaching row 8  The science under this episode’s problem — live.

items.sub: Beginner · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Ray and Maya beside a board. Feedback is the howl when a mic hears its own speaker. Gain before feedback is how loud you can go before it starts. And more open mics make it worse? By minus ten log of how many more. One mic to four: minus ten times log four — about minus six decibels. Mute what nobody's using.

bubbles.text: Feedback is the howl when a mic hears its own speaker. Gain before feedback is how loud you can go before it starts.
And more open mics make it worse?
By minus ten log of how many more. One mic to four: minus ten times log four — about minus six decibels. Mute what nobody's using.

items.caption: Beginner: the term, what it means, the formula — and one worked example out loud.

items.text: 📘 RAY'S NOTEBOOK · BEGINNER  Terms    Feedback   A howl when a microphone picks up its own loudspeaker and the loop gain reaches 0 dB or more.   Gain before feedback   How loud you can make a mic before it starts to ring. Fewer open mics means more of it.   Hearing loop   An assistive listening system that sends audio magnetically to hearing aids.   Formula, variables and a worked example   ƒ FORMULA · Open microphones and gain before feedback  ΔGBF = −10·log 10 (N open )   N open   how many times more mics are open  ΔGBF  change in gain before feedback, dB    Worked example.  Going from 1 open mic to 4: −10·log₁₀(4) ≈ −6 dB of gain before feedback.

📒 EMPATHIA LEARN FIELDBOOK · MODULE 07 OF 31 · PP. 42–43, 111, 149  PART 3 AUDIO FOUNDATIONS  Page 149:  Face the mic. Keep it close.  Ray's margin: “Teach it kindly. Readers aren't the problem. Distance is.”

items.label: **Fieldbook module 7 — Microphones and mic technique.** Beginner support: every new word is defined, and every formula comes with its variables and a worked example.

items.alt: Ray, reading the same label, remembers.

bubbles.text: I patched that. Nine years ago. The wedges were the only mix with speech in it back then.
Then somebody built SPOKEN WORD to mute the wedges.

items.caption: Two good decisions, years apart, that nobody connected. (DEBT-002 grows.)

lines.text: Nine years. I patched it the week my father died. I wasn't thinking about the next person.
(She doesn't know what to say. So she doesn't say anything, and that turns out to be right.)

items.prompt: The listening system rides on the band's monitor mix. How do you fix it?
items.happening: SPOKEN WORD mutes AUX 4, and the listening system hangs off AUX 4.
known: ▮ Receiver silent only in SPOKEN WORD
unknown: What receiver users actually need to hear
timeout: Sunday soundcheck starts with the listening system still on AUX 4.
Two people will miss another reading.

options.label: Unmute AUX 4 in SPOKEN WORD
options.result: The readings come through the receivers — and through the band wedges, into open mics, during the sermon.
options.consequence: A ring of feedback in the quietest moment of the service.
options.fail: Fixing one output by breaking another — feedback in the sermon.

options.label: Give it its own mix
options.result: A dedicated AUX 6 for the listening system: speech and music, never muted by any scene, saved in every preset.
options.consequence: The listening system has its own intent — and its own line in the drawing.

options.label: Feed it from the main mix
options.result: It works, but the main is shaped for a big room, not for an ear an inch away.
options.consequence: Avery, later: “It works. Is it good?” Some speech sounds boomy in the receivers.

options.label: Post a sign: “music only”
options.fail: Excluding people is not a fix.

items.alt: System View after the fix: a new bus, AUX 6 · LISTENING, takes every speech and music input and feeds only the listening transmitter. It is never muted by any scene.
items.caption: AUX 6 · LISTENING: its own mix, its own intent, never muted by a scene.

items.title: Maxwell predicts, Hertz proves
items.body: James Clerk Maxwell's equations of 1865 predicted invisible electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light. In 1887 Heinrich Hertz made sparks jump a gap across his lab and proved them. Dolores's receiver lives on that discovery.

items.alt: Avery, an accessibility and user-experience lead Imani knows, arrives to help. They wear lilac and carry a small notebook.

bubbles.text: Hi, I'm Avery, they/them. Imani says you fixed it. Great — now: is it good?

lines.text: Hi. Avery, they/them. I'm the person who asks “is it good?” after everyone says “it works.”
It's the only job that ever made anyone cry at a sound check.

items.alt: Avery explains how to look at it.

bubbles.text: Dolores doesn't experience a transmitter, a bus and a preset. She experiences one room. Test it the way she lives it.

items.caption: “The user experiences one room, not your org chart.”

items.prompt: How do you prove the listening system works?
items.happening: AUX 6 is built and saved in every preset.

options.label: Check it at the booth
options.consequence: The booth isn't where anyone sits with a receiver.

options.label: Test with users, every scene
options.result: Dolores and Mr. Adeyemi, in their own seats, through the whole service order — and they tell you what they hear.
options.consequence: The proof comes from the people it's for.

options.label: Watch the meter
options.consequence: Signal present isn't the same as speech understood.

items.alt: Thursday evening. Dolores in row 8 and Mr. Adeyemi across the aisle, each with a receiver, while Lily steps through every preset and Ana reads a practice scripture passage.
items.caption: Condition 1: the whole service order, in their own seats.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #7 · AVERY'S LENS  One room, not your org chart  Users experience the whole system as one thing; test it the way they live it.  Dolores doesn't experience a transmitter, a bus and a preset. She experiences one reading she couldn't hear.

items.alt: Mr. Adeyemi takes off his receiver and grins.

bubbles.text: I heard the reading. I've been coming here eleven years. I didn't know there was a reading.

items.alt: Dolores gives Avery a note of her own.

bubbles.text: It's clear. But the sermon is a little quiet next to the songs.
Write that down, Maya. That's the real spec.

items.caption: Maya balances speech against music in AUX 6. Dolores nods.

items.prompt: The sermon is a little quiet next to the songs. I'm sorry — I don't want to be a bother.

options.label: “You're not a bother. You're the spec.”
options.reply: Write that down. She's the spec. Everyone else is an opinion.

items.alt: Sunday. Ana reads the scripture from the lectern.
items.caption: Condition 2: a full room, the real reading.

items.alt: In row 8 Dolores listens on her receiver, eyes closed. Maya sits a few seats down with a receiver of her own.
In the booth, Lily checks the neighbors: the room speakers are unchanged, the band wedges stay quiet during the sermon, and the stream is unchanged.
items.caption: Adjacent checks: nothing next door broke.

items.alt: After the service Dolores comes to the booth.

bubbles.text: Second time this year you've given me my seat back.
Second time this year the room took it.

Avery and Imani talk after the debrief.

bubbles.text: The fix took thirty minutes. The problem took nine years, because nobody who used it was asked.
Then we ask. Every month.

items.title: One page, titled PEOPLE WE DIDN'T ASK
items.body: Receiver users. The hearing loop in the fellowship hall. The Spanish-language service at 1 p.m. The overflow room. The night janitor who listens to rehearsals. The list goes on to the next page.

items.alt: Ray reads the entry and gives one principle.

bubbles.text: An output without an owner is a promise nobody's keeping.

items.alt: Months later: Imani on the phone, a calendar page behind her showing December 24.

bubbles.text: Christmas Eve planning starts now. Lena from the broadcast studio is coming to look at our cameras.

items.caption: Next: *Christmas Eve.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Test every output against the person it's for, in every scene — not just the moment it works. An assistive system needs its own mix and its own owner, and the proof comes from the people who use it.

REFLECTION (optional)  · Two people had stopped expecting to hear the reading, and nobody knew, because they assumed it was them. Hospitality means asking.  Boundary: none of this explains or proves the routing fault.
